sources.title: The Human Central Nervous System
sources.authors: Nieuwenhuys R, Voogd J, van Huijzen C

pathways.name: Dorsal column–medial lemniscus (posterior column–medial lemniscus) pathway
pathways.category: ascending somatosensory / discriminative touch and proprioception
pathways.function: Conveys conscious proprioception, vibration, fine (discriminative) touch and 2-point discrimination from skin and joints to the primary somatosensory cortex.

steps.cellBodies: Dorsal root ganglion (pseudounipolar neurons)
courseVia: dorsal root (medial division, medial dorsal root entry zone)
fasciculus gracilis (below T6) or fasciculus cuneatus (T6 and above)
steps.terminatesIn: Nucleus gracilis (lower body) or nucleus cuneatus (upper body) in caudal medulla

evidence.quote: Root fibres from sacral and lumbar dorsal roots ascend into the fasciculus gracilis; root fibres from cervical roots ascend into the fasciculus cuneatus, to terminate in the corresponding dorsal column nuclei.
Fibres from sacral and lumbar roots ascend medially, in the fasciculus gracilis; those from cervical roots ascend laterally, in the fasciculus cuneatus.
The dorsal column nuclei consist of the medial nucleus gracilis and the more laterally located medial and lateral cuneate nuclei.

steps.cellBodies: Nucleus gracilis / nucleus cuneatus (caudal medulla, dorsal column nuclei)
steps.terminatesIn: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) of thalamus

decussation.where: Internal arcuate fibers cross the midline in the caudal medulla (sensory decussation)

evidence.quote: Fibres from the dorsal column nuclei decussate in the caudal medulla oblongata and ascend into the medial lemniscus to the lateral ventroposterior nucleus of the thalamus.
The dorsal column nuclei project to the contralateral VPL through the medial lemniscus.

steps.cellBodies: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) of thalamus
steps.terminatesIn: Primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2)
steps.laterality: ipsilateral (to thalamus; contralateral to body side of origin)

evidence.quote: The lateral ventroposterior nucleus innervates areas 3 b and 1 of the primary somatosensory cortex and the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2).

conflicts.issue: Level of the boundary between the fasciculus gracilis (lower body) and the fasciculus cuneatus (upper body)

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S7): a fairly sharp segmental cutoff -- gracile fasciculus carries the lower body (T7 and below), cuneate fasciculus the upper body (C2-T7)
positions.source: S7 (original somatosensory.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: The gracile fasciculus conveys sensory information from the lower body (T7 and below) and synapses with the gracile nucleus. The cuneate fasciculus conveys sensory information from the upper body (C2–T7) and synapses to the cuneate nucleus

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys describes a gradual transition rather than a sharp cutoff: sacral/lumbar fibres in the gracile fasciculus, cervical fibres in the cuneate fasciculus, with a small contingent of thoracic fibres occupying an intermediate position between the two
positions.quote: Fibres from sacral and lumbar roots ascend medially, in the fasciculus gracilis; those from cervical roots ascend laterally, in the fasciculus cuneatus. A small contingent of thoracic fibres takes an intermediate position

conflicts.issue: Whether dorsal column lesions actually abolish conscious touch localization and position sense in humans

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S13): dorsal column/posterior column damage causes loss of fine touch, vibration, 2-point discrimination and conscious proprioception
positions.source: S13 (original somatosensory.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: Ipsilateral modalities of fine touch, vibration, 2-point discrimination, and conscious proprioception are affected due to injury to the dorsal columns ascending within the dorsomedial spinal cord

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys states that in patients with dorsal column lesions the localization of tactile stimuli and position sense is mostly intact, implying other ascending spinal systems (e.g. the anterolateral fasciculus) also contribute to these modalities
positions.quote: In patients with lesions of the dorsal columns the localization of tactile stimuli and position sense is mostly intact

unsourced: Glutamate is the excitatory neurotransmitter used at first- and second-order synapses of the DCML pathway (widely stated in standard neuroanatomy texts, but no explicit sourced quote naming the neurotransmitter was found in Nieuwenhuys ch.16).

pathways.name: Anterolateral system / spinothalamic tract
pathways.category: ascending somatosensory / pain, temperature and crude touch
pathways.function: Carries nociceptive, thermal, crude touch and pressure information from the body to the thalamus; includes spinothalamic, spinoreticular and spinotectal (spinomesencephalic) components.

steps.cellBodies: Dorsal root ganglion (pseudounipolar neurons)
steps.terminatesIn: Dorsal horn grey matter – substantia gelatinosa / laminae I, II, V

steps.cellBodies: Dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa / laminae I, II, V)
courseVia: anterolateral/ventrolateral white matter of spinal cord
steps.terminatesIn: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) of thalamus (spinothalamic component); also reticular formation (spinoreticular) and tectum/periaqueductal region (spinotectal/spinomesencephalic)

decussation.where: Anterior white commissure, a few spinal segments above the level of entry

evidence.quote: Most of the fibres joining the anterolateral fasciculus cross in the ventral white commissure, but a distinct ipsilateral component exists.
The spinothalamic tract takes its origin from multiple laminae and from all levels of the spinal cord.

They terminate diffusely in the centrolateral intralaminar nucleus, in the adjoining lateral paralaminar region of the mediodorsal nucleus, and more sparsely, in other intralaminar and midline nuclei of the thalamus

steps.cellBodies: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) of thalamus
steps.terminatesIn: Primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus)
steps.laterality: ipsilateral (to thalamus; contralateral to body side of origin)

conflicts.issue: Which spinal grey-matter laminae give rise to the second-order (spinothalamic) projection neurons

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S8): the relay occurs in the substantia gelatinosa, i.e. laminae I, II and V
positions.source: S8 (original somatosensory.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: Initial pain signals ascend through the dorsal horn, specifically through lamina I (superficial dorsal horn), lamina II (substantia gelatinosa), and lamina V (deep dorsal horn)

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys states the spinothalamic tract arises from lamina I and laminae IV-IX, with most cells actually located in lamina I, the lamina IV/V border zone, lamina VI, and scattered in laminae VII and VIII -- a broader and different set of laminae than I, II, V
positions.quote: Most spinothalamic tract cells occur in lamina I (50% [51]), in the lamina IV/V border zone and lamina VI mostly laterally, and scattered in laminae VII and VIII.

conflicts.issue: Primary thalamic relay nucleus for spinothalamic pain and temperature fibres

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S3): the ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) is the thalamic relay and gives rise to the third-order neurons of this pathway
positions.source: S3 (original somatosensory.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: The spinothalamic tract of the anterolateral system terminates in the ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) of the thalamus, the third-order neurons of this pathway

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys identifies a separate, dedicated nucleus -- the posterior ventromedial nucleus (VMpo) -- as the main relay for pain and temperature; VPL receives only scattered spinothalamic terminations
positions.quote: The main relay nucleus for the conduction of pain and temperature is the VMpo

unsourced: Substance P and glutamate are the principal neurotransmitters of first-order nociceptive afferents synapsing in the dorsal horn (standard teaching; no explicit sourced quote naming the neurotransmitter at spinothalamic synapses was found in Nieuwenhuys ch.16).

pathways.name: Trigeminal somatosensory pathways
pathways.category: ascending somatosensory / face and oral cavity
pathways.function: Transmits pain, temperature, touch, vibration, 2-point discrimination and proprioception from the face and muscles of mastication via three sensory nuclei (principal/chief sensory, spinal trigeminal, mesencephalic) to VPM and the somatosensory cortex.

steps.cellBodies: Trigeminal (semilunar/Gasserian) ganglion (pseudounipolar neurons); mesencephalic nucleus neurons (unique – cell bodies lie within the CNS, not the ganglion)
courseVia: trigeminal nerve root entering brainstem at mid-pons
steps.terminatesIn: Chief/principal sensory nucleus, spinal trigeminal nucleus, or mesencephalic nucleus depending on modality

evidence.quote: Somatosensory fibres of the trigeminal nerve enter the pons in the sensory root (portio major) and are distributed to the principal sensory nucleus and the spinal trigeminal nucleus.
Unlike other primary afferents, the Ia muscle-spindle afferents from the jaw muscles, which enter the brain stem in the trigeminal nerve, arise from cells located within the central nervous system.
The axons of these cells descend into the mesencephalic tract of the trigeminal nerve and then bifurcate.
One branch terminates on the motoneurons of the trigeminal motor nucleus.

steps.cellBodies: Chief/principal sensory nucleus (touch/proprioception/vibration/2-point discrimination) or spinal trigeminal nucleus, pars caudalis (pain/temperature/crude touch)
courseVia: dorsal trigeminothalamic tract (DTTT, ipsilateral, from chief sensory nucleus)
ventral trigeminothalamic tract (VTTT, decussates, from chief sensory nucleus and spinal trigeminal nucleus)
steps.terminatesIn: Ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) of thalamus

decussation.where: Fibers of the ventral trigeminothalamic tract decussate near their nucleus of origin (chief sensory nucleus or spinal trigeminal nucleus) before ascending to VPM

evidence.quote: The principal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve projects bilaterally to the VPM as the trigeminal component of the medial lemniscus and the uncrossed dorsal trigeminothalamic tract
The entire principal sensory nucleus gives rise to a crossed pathway joining the medial lemniscus as the trigeminal lemniscus
The uncrossed dorsal trigeminothalamic tract arises from the dorsal part of the principal sensory nucleus and conducts information from the intraoral cavity
The termination of the uncrossed trigeminothalamic is found in the medial VPM, lateral to the gustatory parvocellular VPM.

steps.cellBodies: Ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) of thalamus
steps.terminatesIn: Primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2)
steps.laterality: ipsilateral (to thalamus; contralateral to face side of origin for pain/temperature)

evidence.quote: VPM projects laterally in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1).

lesions.site: Sjöqvist tractotomy of the spinal trigeminal tract at the rostral border of the pars caudalis
lesions.deficit: Effective elimination of pain and temperature sensitivity in the ipsilateral face, with sparing of tactile sense

evidence.quote: The essential role of the caudal subnucleus in pain and temperature transmission from the face is exemplified by Sjöqvist’s tractotomy of the spinal tract at the level of the rostral border of the pars caudalis
which effectively eliminates pain and temperature sensitivity in the ipsilateral face, leaving the tactile sense intact.

conflicts.issue: Level at which crossed trigeminothalamic fibres decussate

positions.claim: Fibres from the principal sensory nucleus and the pars oralis and interpolaris of the spinal trigeminal nucleus decussate at the level of the pons
positions.quote: Fibres from the principal sensory nucleus and the pars oralis and interpolaris of the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve decussate at the level of the pons and join the medial lemniscus as the trigeminal lemniscus.

positions.claim: Fibres from the pars caudalis (pain/temperature) instead cross in the caudal medulla oblongata before joining the spinothalamic tract -- a different decussation level than the other trigeminal subnuclei
positions.quote: The caudal subnucleus gives rise to ascending fibres, which cross in the caudal medulla oblongata and join the spinothalamic tract

conflicts.issue: Thalamic termination of pars caudalis (pain/temperature) trigeminothalamic fibres

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S5): this tract conveys fast pain and temperature to the contralateral ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM)
positions.source: S5 (original somatosensory.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: This specific tract conveys fast pain and temperature from one side of the face to the contralateral ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM) and eventually to the primary sensory cortex

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys states that pars caudalis trigeminothalamic fibres join the spinothalamic tract and terminate mainly in the intralaminar nuclei, the posterior ventromedial nucleus (VMpo), the caudal medial dorsal nucleus and the shell of the ventroposterior complex -- not primarily VPM
positions.quote: Trigeminothalamic fibres from all layers of the subnucleus caudalis of the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve join the spinothalamic tract to terminate in the intralaminar nuclei, the posterior ventromedial nucleus (VMpo), the caudal medial dorsal nucleus (MD) and the shell of the ventroposterior complex.

pathways.name: Spinocerebellar tracts (dorsal/posterior spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, ventral/anterior spinocerebellar)
pathways.category: ascending somatosensory / unconscious proprioception to cerebellum
pathways.function: Relay unconscious proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs of the trunk and limbs to the cerebellum for coordination of posture and movement.

steps.cellBodies: Dorsal root ganglion (pseudounipolar neurons); axons collateralize to Clarke's nucleus/column (C8–L3) for the trunk and lower limb
courseVia: collateral to posterior grey horn (Clarke's column, C8–L3)
steps.terminatesIn: Clarke's nucleus (dorsal nucleus of Clarke), C8–L3

evidence.quote: Clarkes’s column and the spinal border cells receive dorsal root afferents and give rise to spinocerebellar pathways

An important contingent of sacral and lumbar root fibres, carrying proprioceptive information from the lower limbs, leaves the dorsal columns to terminate in the spinal grey matter, particularly in Clarke’s dorsal column, which gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract

steps.cellBodies: Clarke's nucleus/column (dorsal/posterior spinocerebellar tract, trunk & lower limb) or accessory cuneate nucleus in medulla (cuneocerebellar tract, upper limb equivalent)
courseVia: dorsal (posterior) spinocerebellar tract, ipsilateral lateral funiculus
cuneate fasciculus → accessory cuneate nucleus → inferior cerebellar peduncle (cuneocerebellar tract)
steps.terminatesIn: Ipsilateral cerebellar cortex (vermis and paravermis of anterior lobe) as mossy fibers

evidence.quote: The large, myelinated axons of Clarke’s column occupy the dorsolateral periphery of the lateral funiculus as the uncrossed dorsal spinocerebellar tract
Joined by fibres originating from the reticular formation, the external cuneate nucleus and the contralateral inferior olive, it constitutes the restiform body
composed of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract and of external arcuate fibres from the reticular nuclei of the lateral and anterior funiculus
The restiform body is an afferent system, containing the spinocerebellar and olivocerebellar tracts and other afferents from the medulla oblongata.
The lateral cuneate nucleus and group Z, a collection of large neurons rostral to the gracile nucleus, both receive information from muscle spindle afferents.
Muscle spindle afferents from the forelimb ascend in the dorsal columns and terminate in a somatotopical pattern in the lateral cuneate nucleus.
The main projection of the lateral cuneate nucleus is to the cerebellum.
A rough localization in the paravermal region of the hind limb in the ventral lobules of the anterior lobe

Spinocerebellar fibres distribute to the anterior lobe and certain lobules of the posterior lobe (lobulus simplex, pyramis, lobulus gracilis and the lateral belly of the biventral lobule, the paramedian lobule of comparative anatomy

steps.cellBodies: Ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract neurons (lumbosacral cord)
steps.terminatesIn: Ipsilateral cerebellar cortex (double decussation restores ipsilateral termination)

decussation.where: Decussates once near Clarke's nucleus/level of origin, then decussates again within the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle

evidence.quote: The latter stems from contralateral spinal border cells of the lumbar cord

The ventral spinocerebellar tract leaves the area of the anterolateral fascicle in the rostral metencephalon, and passes rostral to the entrance of the trigeminal nerve to enter the cerebellum along the superior cerebellar peduncle.

conflicts.issue: Precise segmental extent of Clarke's column (dorsal nucleus of Clarke)

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S6): Clarke's column ranges specifically from spinal segments C8 to L3
positions.source: S6 (original somatosensory.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: This set of nuclei range from the C8-L3 portions of the spinal cord, collectively referred to as Clarke’s column

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys describes Clarke's column only in non-numeric terms, as located at 'thoracic and high lumbar levels', without giving C8 or L3 as exact boundaries
positions.quote: is a discrete, roundish collection of large neurons, located medially at the base of the dorsal horn at thoracic and high lumbar levels

unsourced: Nieuwenhuys describes the ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract's origin and course anatomically (arising from contralateral spinal border cells of the lumbar cord) but does not explicitly characterize whether its content is proprioceptive sensory information or motor/efference-copy signalling, so this source cannot adjudicate the existing conflict about the tract's functional content.

Nieuwenhuys does not explicitly state that the ventral spinocerebellar tract decussates a second time within the cerebellum itself; only a general principle that cerebellar hemisphere signs are ipsilateral 'due to the double decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle and the pyramidal tract' was found (Nieuwenhuys ch.20, p.834), which concerns cerebellar output rather than the VSCT specifically.

pathways.name: Descending pain modulation (PAG–RVM–dorsal horn and PAG–locus coeruleus pathways)
pathways.function: Midbrain and brainstem circuits that inhibit (or facilitate) nociceptive transmission at the dorsal horn, via serotonergic PAG–raphe magnus–enkephalinergic interneuron and noradrenergic PAG–locus coeruleus routes.

steps.cellBodies: Periaqueductal gray (PAG), midbrain – receives ascending nociceptive input from dorsal horn lamina I, II, V via spinothalamic/spinobulbar pathways
courseVia: ascending spinothalamic and spinobulbar pathways to PAG
steps.terminatesIn: Periaqueductal gray (dorsal, dorsolateral, lateral, ventrolateral columns)
steps.neurotransmitter: glutamate (ascending); serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, enkephalin, GABA within PAG circuitry

evidence.quote: The mesencephalic periaqueductal grey receives afferents from spinal laminae I, VI, VII and VIII, and projects to the intralaminar thalamic nuclei

steps.cellBodies: PAG neurons projecting to raphe nuclei (rostral ventromedial medulla, including nucleus raphe magnus)
courseVia: PAG → raphe nuclei (glutamatergic) → descending raphespinal fibers to dorsal horn
steps.terminatesIn: Dorsal horn – enkephalinergic interneurons that inhibit C-fiber pain afferents
steps.neurotransmitter: serotonin (PAG–RVM–dorsal horn pathway); glutamate (PAG→raphe activation); enkephalin (dorsal horn interneurons)

evidence.quote: The nucleus raphe magnus contains numerous serotoninergic neurons, and it has been demonstrated that its cells project massively to the superficial dorsal horn

steps.cellBodies: Locus coeruleus (lateral floor of fourth ventricle / upper dorsolateral pons)
courseVia: PAG → locus coeruleus → descending noradrenergic fibers to dorsal horn
steps.terminatesIn: Dorsal horn – presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors on nociceptive afferents

evidence.quote: Noradrenergic cells situated in rhombencephalic catecholaminergic cell groups A5, A6 and A7, which also project to the superficial dorsal horn, contribute to the descending pain-inhibiting system

steps.cellBodies: Dorsal horn inhibitory interneurons (enkephalinergic and other opioid/GABA/glycinergic types) activated by A-beta afferents and by descending PAG/RVM input
steps.terminatesIn: Presynaptic and postsynaptic inhibition of dorsal horn projection neurons of the anterolateral system

evidence.quote: The first of these is the “gate control mechanism”, which was first described by Melzack and Wall
Opiates exert their influence on nociceptive transmission both at the level of the periaqueductal grey and at the termination of the primary afferents.
Specific nociceptive neurons in lamina I are selectively inhibited by morphine

lesions.site: Periaqueductal gray – clinical/experimental stimulation and dysfunction (not a classic named eponymous syndrome)
lesions.deficit: Stimulation of PAG reduces anesthetic/analgesic requirement (antinociception); reduced PAG activation is associated with chronic pain states such as low back pain and complex regional pain syndrome

evidence.quote: This system was first noticed after discovering that electrical stimulation of the mesencephalic periaqueductal grey produces profound analgesia

conflicts.issue: Anatomical source of the noradrenergic descending pain-inhibitory projection to the dorsal horn

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S8): the noradrenergic route is specifically the PAG-locus coeruleus (LC) pathway
positions.source: S8 (original somatosensory.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: The PAG -LC pathway propagates by norepinephrine (NE), exerting an antinociceptive effect in the dorsal horn via the presynaptic alpha-2 receptor

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys attributes the descending noradrenergic pain-inhibiting projection to a broader set of rhombencephalic catecholaminergic cell groups, A5, A6 and A7 (of which the locus coeruleus corresponds only to A6), rather than to the locus coeruleus alone
positions.quote: Noradrenergic cells situated in rhombencephalic catecholaminergic cell groups A5, A6 and A7, which also project to the superficial dorsal horn, contribute to the descending pain-inhibiting system

unsourced: GABAergic and glycinergic interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa mediate presynaptic and postsynaptic inhibition of nociceptive afferents as part of the gate-control mechanism; Nieuwenhuys names and attributes the 'gate control mechanism' to Melzack and Wall but does not explicitly state which transmitter acts presynaptically at the primary afferent terminal.

pathways.name: Lateral and anterior corticospinal tracts
pathways.function: Voluntary control of contralateral limb (lateral tract) and axial/trunk (anterior tract) musculature

steps.cellBodies: Primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, area 4), with contributions from premotor and supplementary motor cortex
steps.terminatesIn: Lateral corticospinal tract: interneurons and alpha motor neurons of the contralateral anterior (ventral) horn; anterior corticospinal tract: axial/proximal motor neurons bilaterally
steps.laterality: ipsilateral until the pyramidal decussation, then contralateral (lateral tract)
steps.neurotransmitter: glutamate (stated for the Ia-afferent/alpha-motor-neuron synapse in the reflex arc; not explicitly named for the corticomotoneuronal synapse in the opened sources)

evidence.quote: Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres from the pericentral cortex descend in the internal capsule and the middle portion of the cerebral peduncle
After traversing the pontine nuclei they form the pyramidal tract on the ventral surface of the medulla oblongata.
Corticospinal fibres decussate at the border of the medulla oblongata with the spinal cord.
The pyramidal tract emerges at the surface at the caudal border of the pons and decussates at the transition of the medulla oblongata with the spinal cord.
The distribution of the corticospinal tract in the human brain is very similar to that in nonhuman primates

steps.cellBodies: Lateral corticospinal tract fibers (>90% of corticospinal fibers by one source; ~70-80% by another, see conflicts)
courseVia: lateral funiculus of the spinal cord
steps.terminatesIn: central gray column and base of dorsal column; either interneurons or directly on lower motor neurons

evidence.quote: After its partial decussation at the border of the brain stem and the cord, the crossed fibres of the pyramidal tract descend into the dorsal half of the lateral funiculus as the lateral pyramidal tract

steps.cellBodies: Uncrossed anterior corticospinal tract fibers
courseVia: anterior funiculus of the spinal cord
steps.terminatesIn: axial and proximal (trunk) motor neurons, bilaterally

decussation.where: crosses locally at the segmental level near termination

evidence.quote: The uncrossed fibres of the anterior pyramidal tract are located in the anterior funiculus, next to the anterior median fissure.

conflicts.issue: Proportion of corticospinal fibres that decussate at the pyramidal decussation

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S1 of motor.json): the lateral (crossed) corticospinal tract contains over 90% of corticospinal fibres
positions.source: S1 (original motor.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: The lateral corticospinal tract contains over 90% of the fibers present in the corticospinal tract and runs the length of the spinal cord.

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S13 of motor.json): almost 70-80% of corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation
positions.source: S13 (original motor.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: At the lower end of the medulla, almost 70 to 80% of the fibers cross to the opposite side of the spinal cord, called the pyramidal (motor) decussation .

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys gives no human percentage at all, describing the human decussation only as 'partial'; the only numeric figure given is for monkeys, where about 10% of the dorsolateral pyramidal tract remains uncrossed (i.e. roughly 90% crossed) -- animal data, not a human measurement
positions.quote: In monkeys 10% of the dorsolateral pyramidal tract is uncrossed, and a similar percentage of the corticospinal fibres terminates ipsilaterally

unsourced: The corticomotoneuronal synapse on alpha motor neurons uses glutamate as its neurotransmitter (physiologically well established but not stated verbatim in Nieuwenhuys ch.21/ch.06).

pathways.name: Corticobulbar (corticonuclear) tract
pathways.function: Upper motor neuron innervation of cranial nerve motor nuclei supplying the head, face, pharynx, larynx and tongue

steps.cellBodies: Precentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 4, 6), premotor and supplementary motor areas
courseVia: crus cerebri of the cerebral peduncle (middle third)
steps.terminatesIn: Motor nuclei of trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, and hypoglossal cranial nerves (directly or via interneurons)
steps.laterality: bilateral for most cranial nerve nuclei

decussation.where: fibers project bilaterally rather than crossing en masse; the lower facial and hypoglossal components are largely crossed

steps.cellBodies: Corticobulbar fibers destined for the facial nucleus
courseVia: as above to the pontine facial motor nucleus
steps.terminatesIn: Dorsal (upper face) division of the facial motor nucleus bilaterally; ventral (lower face) division of the facial motor nucleus contralaterally

decussation.where: lower-face component crosses before reaching the ventral facial subnucleus

evidence.quote: Contrary to the motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, the motoneurons of the facial nucleus receive a strong, bilateral projection from the motor cortex
the face area of M1, the dorsal and ventral premotor cortex and the caudal cingulate motor area project to the contralateral lateral subnucleus that innervates the perioral muscles.
Direct corticomotoneuronal connections to the trigeminal motor nucleus appear to be scarce or absent.

steps.cellBodies: Corticobulbar fibers destined for the hypoglossal nucleus
courseVia: as above to the medullary hypoglossal nucleus
steps.terminatesIn: Hypoglossal nucleus, predominantly contralateral

decussation.where: crosses before reaching the hypoglossal nucleus

evidence.quote: Direct corticomotoneuronal projections to the hypoglossal nucleus are rare in non-human primates, but strengthened in humans

conflicts.issue: Whether sparing of the muscles of mastication after a unilateral corticobulbar lesion reflects abundant direct bilateral corticomotoneuronal wiring to the trigeminal motor nucleus

positions.claim: Original batch (StatPearls, S5): a unilateral cortical lesion does not affect the muscles of mastication because the motor nucleus receives bilateral cortical input
positions.source: S5 (original motor.json batch; not reopened this session)
positions.quote: a unilateral cortical lesion does not affect the muscles of mastication; this is because the motor nucleus receives bilateral cortical input

positions.claim: Nieuwenhuys (citing monkey tracing studies) reports that direct corticomotoneuronal connections onto the trigeminal motor nucleus itself are scarce or absent, implying the bilateral sparing of jaw muscles is mediated indirectly (via brain stem premotor/interneuron circuits) rather than by an abundance of direct bilateral corticomotoneuronal fibres
positions.quote: Direct corticomotoneuronal connections to the trigeminal motor nucleus appear to be scarce or absent.

unsourced: The trigeminal motor nucleus and nucleus ambiguus (vagal/glossopharyngeal motor component) are said to receive predominantly bilateral corticobulbar input, but no source-verified statement specific to the nucleus ambiguus by that name was found in Nieuwenhuys ch.21.

pathways.name: Basal ganglia circuits: direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways
pathways.function: Gate and modulate initiation, amplitude, and suppression of voluntary movement via cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical loops

steps.cellBodies: Cerebral cortex (motor, frontal, parietal lobes, layers III and V)
steps.terminatesIn: Striatum (caudate and putamen) medium spiny neurons

evidence.quote: The corticostriate fibres, which use the excitatory amino acid glutamate as their neurotransmitter

steps.cellBodies: Striatal medium spiny neurons expressing D1 dopamine receptors (direct pathway)
steps.terminatesIn: Globus pallidus internus (GPi) / substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNpr)

evidence.quote: The striatal efferents passing to the GPi arise from medium-sized spiny neurons (MSNs) that co-contain GABA and substance P, whereas the striatal projections to the GPe arise from MSNs that co-contain GABA and enkephalin.

The D1 class receptors are preferentially expressed in the substance P-containing MSNs forming part of the direct circuit, whereas the D2 class receptors are specifically expressed on the enkephalin-containing MSNs
The vast majority of the striatopallidal and striatonigral fibres are known to contain GABA and to exert an inhibitory influence.
The direct circuit is composed of excitatory corticostriatal, inhibitory striatopallidal, inhibitory pallidothalamic and excitatory thalamocortical projections.

steps.cellBodies: GPi / SNpr inhibitory neurons
steps.terminatesIn: Ventral anterior (VA) and ventrolateral (VL) nuclei of the thalamus

evidence.quote: Both the pallidothalamic and nigrothalamic projections are known to be GABAergic
All large neurons within both pallidal segments are GABAergic, inhibitory projection neurons.

The elements in the external segment project to the subthalamic nucleus, whereas those in the internal segment project to the thalamus, the lateral habenular nucleus and the pedunculopontine nucleus in the caudal mesencephalic tegmentum.
They are glutamatergic and activate cortical neurons. As a result of these data the following concept was developed

steps.cellBodies: Striatal medium spiny neurons expressing D2 dopamine receptors (indirect pathway)
steps.terminatesIn: Globus pallidus externus (GPe)

evidence.quote: The indirect circuit includes an excitatory corticostriatal projection that terminates onto striatal medium spiny projection neurons that co-contain GABA and enkephalin along with dopamine D2-class receptors

steps.cellBodies: GPe inhibitory neurons
steps.terminatesIn: Subthalamic nucleus (STN)

evidence.quote: The efferents of the GPe, which are also GABAergic and inhibitory, project in a topographically organized fashion to the subthalamic nucleus (STN)
an inhibitory projection from the GPe to the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and an excitatory projection from STN to the GPi

steps.cellBodies: Subthalamic nucleus neurons (indirect pathway relay)
steps.terminatesIn: GPi / SNpr

evidence.quote: The STN also receives a glutamatergic excitatory input from the cerebral cortex.
The subthalamic efferents have an excitatory effect on pallidal and nigra neurons and use glutamate as their neurotransmitter
The subthalamic neurons are excitatory and use glutamate as their neurotransmitter

cortical activation of the inhibitory, GABA and enkephalin-containing MSNs reduces the output of GPe activity, resulting in a decreased inhibition or disinhibition of STN neurons, which causes an increase in the glutamatergic activation of GPe/SNr.
Cortical activation of the indirect circuit produces disinhibition of subthalamic neurons, resulting in an increase of the subthalamic activation of the GPi.

steps.cellBodies: Sensorimotor cortex (hyperdirect pathway)
steps.terminatesIn: Subthalamic nucleus (dorsal STN) directly, bypassing the striatum

evidence.quote: The subthalamic neurons receive an excitatory, glutamatergic input from the cortex and an inhibitory, GABAergic input from the external pallidal segment.

steps.cellBodies: Substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) dopaminergic neurons (nigrostriatal pathway)
steps.terminatesIn: Putamen and caudate nucleus of the striatum, modulating D1- and D2-expressing neurons oppositely

evidence.quote: The dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta give rise to a large nigrostriatal system, which reciprocates the striatonigral projection.
The striatonigral fibres contain GABA and substance P and inhibit the neurons in the SNc.

lesions.site: Substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons
lesions.deficit: Parkinson disease: bradykinesia, resting tremor, postural instability, shuffling gait (hypokinetic)

evidence.quote: Parkinson’s disease (PD) or paralysis agitans is a common neurodegenerative disorder that usually begins during the fifth or sixth decade of life.
The disease is characterized by progressive slowness of movement (bradykinesia), muscular rigidity, tremor and disturbances in posture and gait.

The neuropathological hallmark of PD is the massive loss of the pigmented, dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra, which leads to a reduction in the dopamine content in the striatum, most severely in the putamen
loss of dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra to the striatum decreases activity in the direct circuit and increases activity in the indirect circuit
Thus, the resultant reduced cortical motor output explains the hypokinetic features of PD.

lesions.deficit: Huntington disease: chorea (hyperkinetic) from interruption of the indirect pathway, plus cognitive and psychiatric dysfunction

evidence.quote: Huntington’s chorea is a rare autosomal dominant disease of middle age, characterized by rapid, jerky, involuntary movements of the face, arms and legs and by progressive mental deterioration.
It has been reported that in the earlier stages of the disease the striatal projection neurons participating in the indirect circuit are preferentially lost

This inhibition of the STN neurons in turn reduces inhibition or disinhibits thalamocortical neurons in V A and VL and, ultimately, increases the excitatory input to the motor cortical areas, which could explain the choreatic movements

lesions.deficit: Hemiballismus: violent, involuntary flinging movements of the ipsilateral (to the lesion side, i.e. contralateral body side) arm and leg

evidence.quote: Hemibalism is a disorder characterized by vigorous involuntary movements of the extremities with a repetitive, stereotypical character on one side of the body.
The hyperkinesia is known to be caused by focal (commonly vascular) lesions of the contralateral STN
It is assumed that the STN lesions reduce the excitation of inhibitory GPi neurons, which in turn causes a hyperactivity of disinhibited thalamocortical projection neurons

pathways.name: Cerebellar circuits: cortico-ponto-cerebellar, olivocerebellar, and cerebellothalamocortical output
pathways.function: Coordinate timing, accuracy, and learning of movement by comparing intended and actual motor output

steps.cellBodies: Cerebral cortex (corticopontine neurons)
steps.terminatesIn: Contralateral cerebellar cortex (mossy fiber input)
steps.laterality: contralateral (relative to the cerebellar hemisphere reached)

decussation.where: pontocerebellar fibers cross in the pons before entering the contralateral middle cerebellar peduncle

evidence.quote: Mossy fibres are excitatory; most use glutamate as their neurotransmitter.
Mossy fibres enter the cerebellum through the restiform body and the middle cerebellar peduncle.
The pontocerebellar projection is mainly crossed; most of its fibres decussate in the pes pontis.

steps.cellBodies: Mossy fiber terminals
steps.terminatesIn: Granule cells, whose parallel fiber axons synapse on Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer

evidence.quote: Granule cell axons ascend toward the molecular layer, where they split into two branches that run parallel to the transverse fissures and, therefore, are called parallel fibres.
Parallel fibres may reach a length of 10 mm or more and terminate with excitatory (glutamatergic) synapses on the spiny branchlets of Purkinje cell dendrites

steps.cellBodies: Inferior olivary nucleus (principal, medial and dorsal accessory olives)

evidence.quote: Climbing fibres originate in the medulla oblongata from the contralateral inferior olive, ascend in the restiform body and distribute to the Purkinje cells
Each adult Purkinje cell is innervated by a single climbing fibre, which terminates with multiple, excitatory (glutamatergic) synapses on the smooth, proximal branches of its dendritic tree.

steps.cellBodies: Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex
courseVia: axons through the granular layer into the cerebellar white matter
steps.terminatesIn: Deep cerebellar (intracerebellar) nuclei: fastigial, interposed (globose/emboliform), and dentate

evidence.quote: Purkinje cells are inhibitory and use gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) as their neurotransmitter
Purkinje cell axons traverse the white matter and terminate on neurons of the cerebellar and certain vestibular nuclei.

Four cerebellar nuclei can be distinguished, which are arranged into two groups of interconnected nuclei: a medial and caudal group, consisting of the fastigial (medial) and the globose (posterior interposed) nuclei

steps.cellBodies: Dentate and interposed (globose/emboliform) nuclei
courseVia: decussation at the level of the inferior colliculus in the midbrain
steps.terminatesIn: Contralateral red nucleus and thalamus (dentato-rubro-thalamic and interposito-rubral tracts)

decussation.where: decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle at the level of the inferior colliculus

evidence.quote: The output of the emboliform, globose and dentate nuclei is directed through the superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum).
The emboliform nucleus (anterior interposed nucleus), which receives Purkinje cell axons of the C1,C 3 and Y zones, projects to the contralateral magnocellular red nucleus and to the thalamus

steps.cellBodies: Fastigial nucleus (vestibulocerebellar output)
steps.terminatesIn: Vestibular nuclei / reticular formation

evidence.quote: Descending pathways to the inferior olive take their origin from the parvocellular red nucleus (the central tegmental tract) and the nuclei of the mesodiencephalic border (the medial tegmental tract)
The central tegmental tract connects the parvocellular red nucleus with the principal olive
gives rise to the central tegmental tract, which takes its origin from the dorsomedial aspect of the red nucleus

One of these tracts, the central tegmental tract , forms a fleece of myelinated fibres around the olive, which is known as the amiculum

lesions.deficit: Ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia ipsilateral to the lesion

Symptoms from damage to the hemisphere and the interposed and dentate nuclei are lateralized to the ipsilateral side due to the double decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle and the pyramidal tract.

pathways.name: Spinal reflex arcs: myotatic, inverse myotatic, and withdrawal reflexes

unsourced: The crossed extensor reflex (contralateral limb extension accompanying ipsilateral flexor withdrawal, mediated by commissural interneurons crossing the spinal midline) is a classic teaching point but was not found described in those terms for LIMB reflexes. Nieuwenhuys does describe an analogous but distinct CERVICAL commissural circuit: 'Commissural interneurons are located in lamina VIII. Their axons cross in the anterior white commissure.' and 'Cervical lamina VIII commissural interneurons use glycine to inhibit contralateral neck motoneurons' (ch.06, p.190-191) -- a glycinergic crossed-inhibitory circuit for the neck, not a generalized crossed-extensor pathway for the limbs.
